newsitem.title: UKRAINE: Ukraine, IMF to pursue talks on three-year funding.
newsitem.headline: Ukraine, IMF to pursue talks on three-year funding.

text.p: Ukraine and the International Monetary Fund will likely pursue talks on a three-year funding programme for the rest of the year, an IMF official said on Wednesday.

"We know decisions need to be made by the end of the year with the Extended Fund Facility (EFF)," resident representative Alex Sundakov told Reuters. "Right now we have the slow gruelling process of identifying measures on each side."
An IMF mission completed a week of work in Kiev on Wednesday and Sundakov said another mission would visit in October or November.
The $2.5-3 billion EFF would succeed Ukraine's $867 million stand-by programme, which is being disbursed in monthly tranches and set to expire at the end of the year.
"Final negotiations for the EFF will take place before the approval deadline," at the end of the year, he said. "Right now it's advance dialogue."
Sundakov said the IMF would announce on Thursday whether Ukraine's next tranche of some $100 million had been approved.

Fund missions have been visiting Ukraine each month to review economic progress and approve monthly disbursements under the stand-by programme. The IMF suspended credits for a time after the government overshot spending targets.

The 1997 budget, aimed at meeting IMF guidelines, calls for inflation to slow to 24.9 percent from a forecast this year of 48 percent and a reduction in the budget deficit to 2.4 percent of gross domestic product by Western calculations.
Sundakov said Ukraine's request for a $1.5 billion currency stabilisation fund for its new hryvnia currency, introduced this month, was still under discussion.
"The question of the currency stabilisation fund is very much tied to the issue of an exchange rate regime," he said.
The central bank has been considering two currency regimes for the hryvnia: a currency corridor or loosely linking it to a currency or basket of currencies.
Central bank officials have appeared confident of receiving the stabilisation fund, which they say is needed for psychological reasons to boost confidence in the new currency.
Ukraine has secured about $2 billion in IMF credits since winning approval for its market reform programme in 1994.
